english.notes:
(i) A disorderly house is a house kept open, not necessarily to the public at large, and so conducted as to violate law and good order. Where the essence of the charge is the presentation of an indecent performance, a conviction for keeping a disorderly house will be supported, although there is no evidence of indecency or disorderly conduct perceptible from the exterior of the house. In order to establish the offence of keeping a disorderly house at common law, the prosecutor must show that the defendant habitually or persistently kept such a house and did so with knowledge of the use to which the premises were put. A single performance of an indecent exhibition has been held to be insufficient to establish the necessary element of habit or persistence to constitute the offence.
(ii) Section 8 of the Disorderly Houses Act 1751 provides that any person who appears, acts or behaves as master or mistress or as the person having the care, government or management of a disorderly house shall be deemed to be the keeper. (In Archbold this legislation is treated as a separate offence to the Common Law and it can be viewed as a separate charge wording at H1701.)
(iii) The owner of a house, letting it out in different apartments to several young women, who use the apartments for the purposes of prostitution, cannot be indicted for keeping a disorderly house. Brothel keeping is normally prosecuted under section 33 of the Sexual Offences Act 1956 - see offence wordings H550 and H554.
